2.  SMT AASHI BHARADWAJ @ AASHI  SHARMA W/O SHRI ABHISHEKH SHARMA  D/O LATE SHRI SANJAY BHARADWAJ R/O  F-1 FIRST FLOOR KAILASH NAGAR  HIMALAYA COMPLEX BAIRAGARH  DISTRICT BHOPAL (MADHYA PRADESH)

 This application coming on for admission this day, the court passed the following:
 ORDER This application under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. has been filed for quashment of FIR No.291/2023 registered at Police Station, Mahila Thana, District Bhopal for offence under Sections 498-A, 506,
34 of IPC and under Sections 3 and 4 of Dowry Prohibition Act.
2. According to the prosecution case, the applicant No.1 is the husband of respondent No.2 whereas the applicant No.2 is the father- in-law and applicant No.3 is the mother-in-law and applicant No.4 is the sister-in-law of respondent No.2. The respondent No.2 has lodged an FIR to the effect she got married to the applicant No.1 on 22.02.2023 as per Hindu Rights and Rituals. It was an arranged marriage and her mother had given sufficient dowry as per her financial capacity. When she came to her matrimonial house, then the applicant No.4 picked up a quarrel with her. Her mother-in-law,
father- in-law started passing taunts on the question of bringing less dowry. Her mother-in-law started pointing out the draw backs in her every work and started torturing her mentally. Her husband was also fighting with her on the question of money. Her husband is an alcoholic and under the influence of alcohol, he used to quarrel with her and used to beat her. Her husband,
mother-in-law, father-in-law and sister-in-law used to allege that her parents have given a less dowry as a result, they have lost their reputation in the society and therefore the respondent No.2 should bring a Car and an amount of Rs.5,00,000/- apart from giving her entire salary. They were also demanding that the house of her parents be also transferred in their name. When it was objected by her, then the applicants started abusing her filthily and they also started making allegations against her character. Her husband also used to beat her and also used to extend her threat. They also use to turn out of her matrimonial house. The applicants were alleging that she should come back only after the dowry is arranged. On 28.04.2023, when she informed her mother on phone, then her mother and other family members came to her matrimonial house to convince the applicants, but the applicants also used filthy language against her family members and in front of her family members, the applicant No.4 also assaulted her. When her brother tried to intervene,
Abhishek Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49565592/
2 then he too was assaulted by her husband. Her parents requested the applicants to allow the respondent No.2 to reside in her matrimonial house but they refused to do so and accordingly, on 29.04.2023 she came back to her parental home. At Bhopal also she received telephonic call from her husband and on phone also her husband demanded an amount of Rs.5,00,000/-. On account of the physical and mental cruelty, the respondent No.2 has suffered a lot. Although, the respondent No.2 tried to save her marital life but the applicants are not ready to listen to her. She also took assistance of Mahila Parmarsh Kendra, Police Station Mahila Thana, Bhopal but the applicants did not change their behavior and accordingly the FIR was lodged. 
3. Challenging the FIR in question, it is submitted by counsel for applicant that the allegations are vague, omnibus and general in nature. The applicant No.4 is the sister-in-law of respondent No.2 and it is well establish principle of law that for prosecuting the near and dear relative of the husband of the complainant, the allegations should be specific and clear. 
4. Per contra, the counsel for State submitted that allegations prima facie make out an offence against all the applicants. 
5. Considered the submissions made by counsel for parties.
6. So far as the applicant No.4 is concerned, she is the sister-in- law of the respondent No.2,
therefore allegations against her should be specific and clear and should not be vague, omnibus and general in nature. If the allegations made in the FIR are considered in the light of the judgment passed by Supreme Court in the case of of Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, reported in (2000) 5 SCC 207, Monju Roy v. State of W.B., (2015) 13 SCC 693, Chandralekha & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan &
Anr. reported in 2013 (1) UC 155, Geeta Mehrotra Vs. State of U.P. reported in (2012) 10 SCC 741,
Preeti Gupta Vs. State of Jharkhand, reported in (2010) 7 SCC 667 is considered, then it is clear that there are specific allegations that on 28.04.2023, when her mother and family members came to the matrimonial house of the respondent No.2, in order to pursue and convince her in-laws, then the applicant No.4 apart from the other applicants used filthy and abusive language against her parents and in front of her parents applicant No.4 assaulted the respondent No.2. When the brother of the respondent No.2 tried to intervene in the matter, then her husband assaulted her brother also. 
There are specific allegations that on demand of dowry, the applicant No.2 was harassing the respondent No.2 physically as well as mentally. The marriage took place on 22.02.2023 and the respondent No.2 was ousted from her matrimonial house on 29.04.2023 i.e. within two months and seven days of marriage. Therefore, in the considered opinion of this Court, there are specific allegations against the applicant No.4 warranting her prosecution for the offences mentioned above. 
7. So far as the allegations against the applicants No.1, 2 and 3 are considered, the Supreme Court in the case of Taramani Parakh v. State of M.P., reported in (2015) 11 SCC 260 has held as under:-
12. In Kailash Chandra Agrawal v. State of U.P. [Kailash Chandra Agrawal v. State of U.P., (2014) 16 SCC 551] , it was observed (SCC p. 553, paras 8-9):
Abhishek Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49565592/
3 "8. We have gone through the FIR and the criminal complaint. In the FIR, the appellants have not been named and in the criminal complaint they have been named without attributing any specific role to them. The relationship of the appellants with the husband of the complainant is distant. In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab [Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 :
(2000) 3 SCR 662] it was observed (SCC p. 217, para 5):
"5. ... A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in-laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits. In their overenthusiasm and anxiety to seek conviction for maximum people, the parents of the deceased have been found to be making efforts for involving other relations which ultimately weaken the case of the prosecution even against the real accused as appears to have happened in the instant case." 
The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material. Only the husband, his parents or at best close family members may be expected to demand dowry or to harass the wife but not distant relations, unless there is tangible material to support allegations made against such distant relations. Mere naming of distant relations is not enough to summon them in the absence of any specific role and material to support such role. 
9. The parameters for quashing proceedings in a criminal complaint are well known. If there are triable issues, the Court is not expected to go into the veracity of the rival versions but where on the face of it, the criminal proceedings are abuse of Court's process, quashing jurisdiction can be exercised. Reference may be made to K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar [K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, (2000) 8 SCC 547 :
2001 SCC (Cri) 27] , Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate [Pepsi Foods Ltd. v.
Judicial Magistrate, (1998) 5 SCC 749 : 1998 SCC (Cri) 1400] , State of Haryana v.
Bhajan Lal [State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri)
426 :
AIR 1992 SC 604] and Asmathunnisa v. State of A.P. [Asmathunnisa v. State of A.P.,
(2011) 11 SCC 259 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 159] "
13. In the present case, the complaint is as follows:
"Sir, it is submitted that I was married on 18-11- 2009 with Sidharath Parakh s/o Manak Chand Parakh r/o Sarafa Bazar in front of Radha Krishna Market, Gwalior according to the Hindu rites and customs. In the marriage my father had given gold and silver ornaments, cash amount and household goods according to his capacity. 
After the marriage when I went to my matrimonial home, I was treated nicely by the members of the family. When on the second occasion I went to my matrimonial home, my husband, father-in-law and mother-in-law started harassing me for not bringing the dowry and started saying that I should bring from my father 25-30 tolas Abhishek Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49565592/
4 of gold and Rs 2,00,000 in cash and only then they would keep me in the house otherwise not. On account of this my husband also used to beat me and my father-in-law and my mother-in-law used to torture me by giving the taunts. In this connection I used to tell my father Kundanmal Oswal, my mother Smt Prem Lata Oswal, uncle Ashok Rai Sharma and uncle Ved Prakash Mishra from time to time. On 2- 4-2010 the members of the family of my matrimonial home forcibly sent me to the house of my parents in Ganj Basoda along with my brother Deepak. They snatched my clothes and ornaments and kept with them. Since then till today my husband has been harassing me on the telephone and has not come to take me back. Being compelled, I have been moving this application before you. Sir, it is prayed that action be taken against husband Sidharath Parakh, my father-in-law Manak Chand Parakh and my mother-in-law Smt Indira Parakh for torturing me on account of demanding dowry."
14. From a reading of the complaint, it cannot be held that even if the allegations are taken as proved no case is made out. There are allegations against Respondent 2 and his parents for harassing the complainant which forced her to leave the matrimonial home. Even now she continues to be separated from the matrimonial home as she apprehends lack of security and safety and proper environment in the matrimonial home. The question whether the appellant has in fact been harassed and treated with cruelty is a matter of trial but at this stage, it cannot be said that no case is made out. Thus, quashing of proceedings before the trial is not permissible."
8. There are specific allegations against the applicants No.1, 2 and 3 about commission of physical and mental cruelty apart from demand of dowry. 
9. It is further submitted by counsel for applicant that an agreement was entered into between the applicant No.1 and respondent No.2 on 28.04.2023, in which no allegation of cruelty was leveled against respondent No.2. 
10. Why the situation arose for executing the agreement within a period of two months from the date of marriage itself speaks in volumes. The things were not normal and therefore occasion had arisen for executing agreement. From the agreement, it is clear that the intentions of the parties were not to break up the marital ties immediately and thus if they had decided to take some time to improve their behavior, then it cannot be said that the respondent No.2 should have mentioned each and every allegation in the agreement. 
11. Furthermore, the FIR was lodged on 02.10.2023 whereas the agreement was executed on 29.04.2022 and the parties had decided to give six months time to re-think about their decision. If the applicant No.1 or the other applicants decided not to improve the things and ultimately when the respondent No.2 found that the things are not going to improve and only thereafter if she lodged an FIR, then it cannot be said that the FIR was lodged on the basis of afterthought allegations. 
Non-mentioning of the allegations in the agreement indicates that the first attempt of the respondent No.2 was to save her marital life. 
Abhishek Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49565592/
5 12. It is further submitted by counsel for the applicants that the applicant No.1 had filed an application under Section 9 of Hindu Marriage Act for restitution of conjugal rights on 19.07.2023 and only thereafter the FIR was lodged by way of counter blast. 
13. The aforesaid submission cannot be accepted in the light of judgment passed by the Supreme Court in the case of Pratibha v. Rameshwari Devi, reported in (2007) 12 SCC 369.
14. The Supreme Court in the case of Pratibha (supra) has held as under:-
"14. From a plain reading of the findings arrived at by the High Court while quashing the FIR, it is apparent that the High Court had relied on extraneous considerations and acted beyond the allegations made in the FIR for quashing the same in exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code. We have already noted the illustrations enumerated in Bhajan Lal case [1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri)
426] and from a careful reading of these illustrations, we are of the view that the allegations emerging from the FIR are not covered by any of the illustrations as noted hereinabove. For example, we may take up one of the findings of the High Court as noted hereinabove. The High Court has drawn an adverse inference on account of the FIR being lodged on 31-12- 2001 while the appellant was forced out of the matrimonial home on 25-5-2001. 
15. In our view, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the appellant wife for lodging the FIR on 31-12- 2001 on the ground that she had left the matrimonial home at least six months before that. This is because, in our view, the High Court had failed to appreciate that the appellant and her family members were,
during this period, making all possible efforts to enter into a settlement so that Respondent 2 husband would take her back to the matrimonial home. If any complaint was made during this period, there was every possibility of not entering into any settlement with Respondent 2 husband. 
16. It is pertinent to note that the complaint was filed only when all efforts to return to the matrimonial home had failed and Respondent 2 husband had filed a divorce petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. 
That apart, in our view, filing of a divorce petition in a civil court cannot be a ground to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code as it is well settled that criminal and civil proceedings are separate and independent and the pendency of a civil proceeding cannot bring to an end a criminal proceeding even if they arise out of the same set of facts. Such being the position, we are, therefore, of the view that the High Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code has gone beyond the allegations made in the FIR and has acted in excess of its jurisdiction and,
therefore, the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by going beyond the allegations made in the FIR or by relying on extraneous considerations. 
Abhishek Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 5 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49565592/
6 22. For the reasons aforesaid, we are inclined to interfere with the order of the High Court and hold that the High Court in quashing the FIR in the exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code by relying on the investigation report and the findings made therein has acted beyond its jurisdiction. For the purpose of finding out the commission of a cognizable offence, the High Court was only required to look into the allegations made in the complaint or the FIR and to conclude whether a prima facie offence had been made out by the complainant in the FIR or the complaint or not." 
15. Thus as already pointed out, the respondent No.2 may not have reproduced the allegations in the agreement in order to save her marital life and once she found that the applicant No.1 has already approached the Court thereby making her life difficult, then if she decided to lodged the FIR, then it cannot be said that the FIR was lodged by way of counter blast. Even otherwise, the findings given by the Civil Court are not binding on the criminal Court and both the proceedings are to be decided independent to each other on the basis of the allegations made therein. 
16. No other argument is advanced by the counsel for applicant. 
17. Considering the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, this Court is of considered opinion that prima facie case is made out warranting prosecution of the applicants for offence under Section 498-A, 506 and 34 r/w Section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act. 
18. The application fails and is hereby dismissed. 
(G.S. AHLUWALIA) JUDGE VB* VINAY KUMAR BURMAN 2024.04.10 18:58:16 +05'30'
